Our Qutrit- based quantum simulator for scalar QED in 2D experiences reduced sQED contributions, with theory calculations showing a shift sQED / sQD of approximately -0.04, leading to a 10% improvement in the agreement between our model and experimental data, reflecting a significant improvement over previous sQD approximations.

Theoretical predictions indicate that when positrons are produced at a high density through strong-field quantum electrodynamics processes, they will exhibit spin polarization. This characteristic can be used in particle physics research and fundamental spin physics. However, existing positron sources struggle to meet the necessary spin polarization and intensity requirements. In an experiment designed to meet these criteria using short, high-energy laser pulses and thin foil targets, researchers successfully generated densely spin-polarized positrons with an electron energy of 1.6 MeV, a polarization of 20%, and an overall production efficiency of 0.1%. This level of performance corresponds to 10^12 positrons per second per milliCoulomb of laser pulse repetition rate around 10Hz. When specifically targeting electron-nucleus collisions, this source demonstrated performance of 10^-4 (s^-1 W^-1) for electron production, resulting in 1.6 MeV electrons per second when using 5-Joule laser pulses at a 10Hz repetition rate.

A group G is said to have algebraic diameter 3 when there exist three elements a, b, and c within the group's conjugacy classes such that the identity is only reachable by combining one element from each class. This study classifies all finite groups with diagonal-3, providing a list of possible groups including SL2, PSL2, An, A(n-1), and An-1 for various values of n.

To fill the gap with existing solutions, a new temperature detector has been created that offers performance characteristics based on voltage and temperature performance. The new approach offers a proportional-to-absolute temperature (PTAT) voltage generation method utilizing a novel full-swing current mirror, resulting in enhanced speed and reduced area consumption. The new detector's performance has been evaluated through simulations, revealing its ability to operate with remarkable precision and efficiency. The new detector's performance has been demonstrated through its ability to achieve a low power consumption and temperature resolution.

We introduce a geometric framework based on Lie groupoids to construct various geometric structures on smooth stacks, specifically the $n$-connection on principal bundles, Chern-Simons forms, and characteristic classes. This framework allows us to define these concepts intrinsically and compute them explicitly, taking into consideration the case of higher groupoids for $n$-connections.

Non-optical continuum research reveals emerging core structures within molecular dense cores, which are critical components in the formation of stars. A star with a mass of 1.4 times that of the sun was recently discovered by breaking through the cloud of the Dragon infrared dark nebula, and its formation process is particularly intriguing as it involves high-mass stars. We investigated this formation process in depth and found that a core structure, specifically component C, existed at the site of the high-mass star before its birth. This core structure was detected and measured, and found to be 1400 astronomical units across and having a temperature of 27 Kelvin. The gas within this core structure was heated by a protostar that was hidden from view and estimated to have a mass of 1.4 times that of the sun. The gas heating pattern of this protostar, along with another one known as G237.65+0.2, indicated both were located deep within component C. These findings suggest that high-mass stars can form within core structures of IDNs, even as they are surrounded by gas that can re-radiate heat.

Recurrence methods have been widely used in Monte Carlo simulations to limit unnecessary distance calculations between random pairs. These techniques are particularly beneficial in scenarios involving a large number of particles. However, in Monte Carlo simulations of field particles, where total particles equal the product of a particle number and a volume recurrence limitations no longer apply. This paper investigates a stochastic model that generates a uniform distribution of a uniform positive definite field on a sphere in three-dimensional space. The amount of field is determined by the product of three independent random numbers raised to certain powers. We discover that the coordinates of such a field can be limited to a single step of a random walk to ensure uniform distribution. This uniformity in step size, particularly the presence of step size one, may offer computational benefits in certain situations.

The friction between solid surfaces is a complex phenomenon with numerous underlying mechanisms. Researchers have developed various models to describe and predict frictional behavior, but these models often require extensive material-specific data. In contrast, the dynamics of polymeric dry foams exhibit striking similarities to dry friction, featuring both static and movement-related friction. Notably, the foams' static friction is influenced by their bubble patterns, leading to a new class of solvable problems in statistics and statistical mechanics that explore the interplay between random properties and local interactions.

This research focuses on classifying skin lesions into benign nevi and malignant melanoma using a dataset of 13500 images. To address the problem, we first extract image features using a ResNet-50 deep neural network, and then employ a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to perform classification. To further improve the SVM's performance, we incorporate an anomaly detection method based on the Least Square Support Vector Clustering (LS-SVC) to identify and remove outlier images. Additionally, we utilize a Kullback-Leibler Entropy (KL-Ent) measure to rank and distinguish between benign and malignant images. Experimental results on a public dataset demonstrate that our proposed approach effectively achieves accurate classification of skin lesions.

A Hele-Shaw cell experiment involving a rapidly spinning, viscous fluid and an injected, air-foam interface was conducted. When the fluid's rotation rate surpassed a critical threshold, a injected interface that was initially uniform became unstable and formed flexible fingers. The width of these fingers depended on the ratio of injection rate to rotation and their tails wrapped around in the direction of rotation due to drag from the surrounding fluid. The injected interface could either stay outside or inside the largest finger's tip, creating two distinct patterns that were differentiated by the size of the injection rate. The ratio of finger size to the largest finger also followed two sets of scaling laws, corresponding to the inside and outside interface configurations. The flexible fingers persisted as the interface moved from the center to the edge of the Hele-Shaw cell. Theoretical models were developed to account for the relationship between the interface and the largest finger, as well as the transition between the two interface configurations.

A peculiar atmospheric anomaly on Earth, stratospheric acetylene and cyanogen levels, spurred a similar investigation of the interstellar cloud TMC-1 in 2021. By analyzing high-resolution radio spectra from the IRAM 30m and IRAM NOEMA 125m telescopes, researchers identified three previously unidentified cyanogen and ethynyl compounds, among them, two new ethynyl ring compounds, ethynyl cyclopropane and ethynyl cyclopentadiene. By comparing observed line intensities with a radiative transfer and statistical equilibrium model, their absolute abundances were determined. Notably, the ethynyl cyclopropane to cyano cyclopropane abundance ratio is approximately 0.1, and the log squared ratio of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene to cyano cyclopentadiene abundance is approximately -0.3. These findings support prior suggestions that ethynyl and cyano derivatives of hydrocarbon rings have comparable abundances in interstellar clouds, providing a basis for future chemical modeling.

Neural machine translation systems with attention mechanisms excel at individual cases, yet they struggle for consistency when translating longer sentences. Even more so, they lack reliability when sentences contain future references that require predictions. We introduce a new attention model, called Look-forward Attention (LFA), which incorporates predicted word probabilities into its planning process. LFA enables the system to anticipate upcoming words, aligns source sentences more accurately, and generates more consistent outputs for sentence lengths. We validate the effectiveness of LFA by value-add experiments on the basis of a top-tiering end-to-end system, demonstrating improved results with simple attention replacement and gaining 5 to 10 points in multiple metrics for a target sentence length of 10 words.

The framework concept has been widely adopted across various domains, yet its implementation specifics have been underexamined. This research investigates how translators transformed the framework concept into a functional tool through the development of Grid Software. By applying Dan Suthers' knowledge mapping method, we analyzed 1,440 pages of whiteboard diagrams, source code, and technical documentation. Our study reveals that three key translatable elements - syntax, semantics, and operational logic - drove the creation of Grid Software. This finding offers a novel perspective on software project evolution, connecting the concept of formal translations to the progression of a software framework.

A new variant of dark sector model, called the Combined Dark Fluid model, is proposed, consisting of two non-interacting fluid components with distinct but comparable dissipative characteristics. A suitable choice of these interaction rates facilitates the intermixing of the fluid components, leading to a non-separable and interactive dark sector. The intermixing of the components results in combined fluid dynamics, allowing for a more robust description of dark sector behavior. A detailed analytical and numerical investigation of the model's dark matter halo formation is carried out, revealing that intermixing has a minimal impact on halo formation, while a more significant one is observed for the Hubble diagram residuals. The model exhibits 2.14 reduced chi-squared value for dark energy parameters, placing it well within the 1-sigma confidence interval, making it an improved version of non-interacting combined dark fluid model.

Neutrino and dark energy theories are proposed beyond the Standard Model, potentially mediated by higher-dimensional operators within the effective field theory framework. By analyzing $J/\psi$ decays into invisible particles, researchers have set new limits on three-dimensional operators linked to neutrino masses, specifically achieving a constraint of $10^{-6}$ on the neutrino mass scale. Additionally, stringent bounds are placed on axion-like particles, including a parameter combination of $10^{6}$ GeV for neutral neutrino interactions and a parameter combination of $10^{10}$ GeV for electroweak interactions. The study also explores charged interactions, resulting in a bound of $10^{-12}$ for parameter combinations involving electron and neutrino. For dark matter production, the findings indicate that a specific dark matter mass range of 1.2 to 1.3 GeV could lead to an underestimation of the cosmic microwave background if a fraction of neutrinos are dark matter and decays into charged particles occur. The analysis further establishes constraints on dark matter-ds neutrino scattering, specifically a limit of $10^{-29}$ cm³/s is set for a scenario where dark matter is composed of neutrino-like particles.

This research introduces a multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) method, building on existing singular spectrum analysis (SSA) techniques. We adapted MFSSA to various dimensional frameworks, including univariate, multivariate, and functional domains, and compared its efficiency against current models using Monte Carlo simulations. Our empirical examination of multivariate temperature evolution patterns in the US during the 20th and 21st centuries demonstrated that MFSSA offers superior predictive accuracy, outperforming standard SSA, multivariate extension, and a long-shortest embedded kernel method.

A key property of one-dimensional random walk is global persistence for local duration. This means that if the walk stays within a limited area for an extended period of time, all points within that area are visited by the walk with an equally high probability. Conversely, there's a high likelihood that the walk will never reach some points within that area. We establish the exact formula for this probability and determine its range for various starting positions of the walk. A preliminary result from an earlier study is also generalized here.

The IShTAR plasma experiment is based on a helicon plasma source that has three modes of operation, with the two-layered helicon mode being the second most commonly used. In this mode of operation, helicon waves are generated in a separate vessel from a magnetically insulated anode (MIA) mode before being transferred to the main chamber through a waveguide. In order to utilize the helicon mode effectively, it is crucial to have a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of helicon plasma and the influence of various parameters on plasma properties. To date, research on helicon plasma sources has been conducted, with some sources utilized for magnetically confined plasma discharges and others for high-density plasma production for etching and deposition processes. On the IShTAR plasma device, which is designed for low-density plasma research, helicon source parameters such as RF power, magnetic field, and gas flow rate can be varied to a wide range. To date, initial investigations on the helicon mode have been carried out, with the help of a Langmuir probe, the characteristics of plasma have been measured. To further investigate helicon plasma properties, a plasma simulation code has been used to replicate the measured plasma properties and predict the influence of various source parameters on plasma properties.

The microscopic examination of tissue samples is a fundamental method for diagnosing diseases, and it relies heavily on the ability of pathologists to identify cell nuclei within images.  Despite its importance, this process is time-consuming and subjective, and it requires highly skilled professionals.  To address this challenge, numerous algorithms have been developed to automate nucleus detection in tissue images.  Many of these methods involve multiple, computationally expensive steps, and they often struggle with small nuclei.  To overcome these limitations, our proposed W-Net model uses a single, unified convolutional network to achieve nucleus detection.  This innovative approach eliminates the need for multiple, separate network stages, and it allows for efficient and accurate detection of nuclei of all sizes.  Experimental results show that our proposed model outperforms the state-of-the-art, and it demonstrates superior performance in detecting small nuclei.  The results of these experiments are presented and discussed in detail.

For any prime $l \geq 3$ and an odd positive integer $s$, we establish the converse Mellin transform theorem for the symplectic group Sp_{2s} and the special orthogonal group of type Sp_{s} or sO_{3s/2} for any $\delta$ relatively prime to $l$.

We present a fundamental explanation of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) by connecting them to matched filtering techniques, which allows for the derivation of the GCNN operation. This enables the step-by-step simulation of GCNN operations and, consequently, the performance of actual GCNNs. To further our understanding, this framework also facilitates the prediction of GCNN outcomes without executing the algorithm.

By reformulating the theory through a Chern-Simons approach, we established that a specific type of scalar field, defined by its first-order equations of motion, can be seamlessly described using General Relativity coupled to a U(1) Chern-Simons gauge field in three dimensions. Leveraging this reformulated theory, we successfully described rotating hairy black holes and black hole solitons, and derived their masses and angular momenta. Our analysis revealed that when the mass and angular momentum are expressed in terms of the boundary conformal field theory parameters, the resulting scaling patterns closely resemble those observed in the universal minimal model. Furthermore, our reformation strategy can be applied to other gauge groups, thereby broadening its applicability.

Medical elastography imaging is a key tool for distinguishing between solid tumors and cystic lesions in the human body. Medical imaging devices often utilize shear waves that move perpendicular to the surface of the patient's skin to create these images. To make elastography images more accurate and useful for surgery planning, it is crucial to measure how layers of tissue move sideways using precise techniques. A new method called virtual shear wave synthetic aperture (vSWA) is presented in this research to improve the measurement of sideways movement using synthetic aperture elastography. Unlike the standard synthetic aperture method, vSA can create waves in both directions along the path of the scan, allowing for a more complete and accurate measurement of sideways movement in three dimensions. When compared to the standard synthetic aperture method, vSWA provides a more precise and reliable measurement of how layers of tissue move sideways, with a correlation coefficient of 0.997 and a standard deviation of 0.006mm. This makes the vSWA technique a promising approach for creating precise medical elastography images.

We introduced the concept of Rational Pseudocode, formalizing algorithms as human-like explanations linked to demonstrations, drawn from the perspective of rational agents. This approach applies Pseudocode, while considering its limitations and enhancing it with background knowledge and contextual cues. Notably, our method can rederive traditional algorithmic formulations, such as those for vector operations, statistical analysis, graph theory, and dynamic programming.

Gaussian data streams with high dimensions are being continuously monitored, and a multivariate normal distribution is assumed. The task involves grouping these data points into $k$ groups based on group means, and the resulting labels are not necessarily unique. To make this problem more manageable, it is being framed within limited settings regarding memory usage and group label comparison, with comparisons to recent research on large-scale group learning and clustering in high dimensions showing similarity. In a recent study, three algorithms are introduced to solve this problem for different group dimensions, showing better performance than the current record in one of the scenarios and improving performance in the other two. These advancements are based on utilizing transformations of the data to reduce their dimensions, combined with techniques for estimating covariance in reduced dimensions.

To enhance the efficiency of integrating autonomous vehicles into traffic systems, reducing the ability of evaders to obstruct their progress is crucial. This work formulates a novel hierarchical variation of the stochastic pursuit-evasion competition, where the pursuer can choose between aggressive pursuit, risking greater damage, or passive pursuit, minimizing harm. Two primary research areas investigate this setup: first, an optimal control method is developed to determine the pursuer's best strategy given any evader approach; and second, game theory principles are applied to identify equilibrium strategy profiles for both players. Numerical results from simulated interactions between intelligent agents illustrate both the effectiveness of the developed policy in equilibrium and the significant impact of excessive damage on the evader's behavior.

A comprehensive framework has been developed to efficiently calculate precise predictions for standard model processes involving one or more vector bosons at tree level within high-energy muon colliders. By leveraging the properties of vector boson tagging and factorization, these calculations can be used to efficiently calculate one-loop QCD corrections in this specific class of processes, including events with one or more vector bosons and light quarks alongside final-state electrons or muons. By employing an established formalism, this calculation framework can be easily applied to a wide range of vector boson factorized partons, enhancing its versatility. The framework has been applied to select processes that are promising for direct vector boson lepton fusion (VLLF) vector boson fusion (VLF) vector boson associated production vector boson scattering (VBS) vector boson quark scattering (VQS) vector boson quark annihilation (VQA). By comparing efficient predictions to PYTHIA8 simulations, the framework shows superior accuracy and speed for a wide range of vector boson transverse momentum distributions. These calculations can be utilized to identify optimal vector boson tagging strategies and design vector boson colliders.

Combining multiple models in multi-task reinforcement learning can lead to conflicting information, where models that perform well on specific tasks negatively impact each other. This study explores the integration of multiple non-linear models for policy prediction in multi-task settings, showing that simply averaging these models degrades overall performance. To overcome this limitation, we developed a modular framework that integrates models without mutual interference, allowing the system to achieve superior or equivalent results to the best individual model across various single and double-task scenarios. Our results indicate that our system can outperform the best single model in up to 80% of test cases. Moreover, we identified the key components necessary for combining models effectively and demonstrated that a critical aspect of our system is the ability to route inputs to the most suitable model. Our modular multi-task system code is available online at this repository: https://github.com/andrewjroberts/modular-rl.

This Godel-Journaal entry re-creates Leslie Journaal's lively presentation, which delves into formal logic's foundational elements as exemplified by Godel, Tarski, and Carnap's work on incompleteness, semantic truth definitions, and induction. We examine formal theories' self-reference capabilities using the CGT induction lemma, which enables first-order formulations of "for all finite levels" induction. Building on this, Tarski's truth definition deficit and Godel's first incompleteness theorem for primitive recursion are demonstrated. Furthermore, we explicitly show how Godel's famously contentious refutation of formalism can be replicated within the higher-level theory $Q$'s framework.

This research extends the Three Spheres Theorem from holomorphic functions to Morse functions on Cliford analysis, focusing specifically on the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. Initially, a three circles principle is established for cliford functions, enabling the interpolation of norm values at three radii within an intermediate range. Subsequently, the three spheres theorem is applied to a particular class of smooth functions, demonstrating that if a function satisfies certain conditions, it can be bounded using values from exponential decay factors relative to the spheres' radii. Additionally, a relation is derived between the $k$-th coefficient of the Gaussian part's Taylor series expansion and the $k$-th Cliford coefficient. The study also incorporates a comparison with a related result from previous work, which pertains to the square of a complex function rather than its square root.

Inverse problem resolution often involves imparting Bayes' network with its prior to generate images consistent with observed data. Our goal is to obtain conditional samples that adhere to both observed data and their corresponding prior. Our proposed method, the Regularized Conditional GAN (RCGN), builds upon the traditional GAN framework by incorporating a regularization term to ensure conditional consistency during posterior issue resolution. Our research indicates that the GCN framework can be adapted to different parameterizations, including those that alter the target distribution or the generator's behavior in response to changing parameters. Our results, compared with existing methods, demonstrate the RCGN's efficacy in maintaining both data consistency and a topological relationship between generated images and their parameterizations.

This research paper investigates the conditions under which invariant manifolds exist in dynamical systems with fractional-order dynamics. Specifically, we examine the dynamics of n-dimensional systems with a linear component and identify the conditions under which invariant surfaces exist. It is demonstrated that, in general, such surfaces do not exist, except in a few particular cases. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which two-dimensional invariant surfaces exist for four-dimensional systems with linear components.

Using scintillometry data from the bright pulsar, B1133+16 over the past two decades, researchers have analyzed how the interstellar environment varies over time at the pulsar's location. A team applied long-term decimetric observations from the VLA and Arecibo observatory to track changes in the time-varying interstellar scintillation pattern around the pulsar. After accounting for the movements of the Earth, the Sun, and the pulsar, they focused on slow changes caused by the stars' movement through the interstellar environment. A significant discovery was made when a change in scintillation pattern, likely caused by encountering a flow of plasma, was noted in November 2020. An examination of observations from VLA in both L and S frequency bands revealed that the Arecibo observatory's data matched. This allowed for an estimation of the size and electron density of a specific region of plasma that the pulsar had just entered. Further investigation into the statistics of interstellar scintillation revealed that the distribution of scattering measures had changed over time, likely due to the pulsar's entry into a region of higher turbulence, possibly within a supernova remnant.

A Deep Neural Network generative model called WaveNet has been widely used for its ability to generate human speech, music, and other types of human voice.  However, WaveNet's high computational cost is primarily due to binary dilated convolution operations that have limited capacity.  In this study, we explore periodic variations in signal components in response to pitch changes and develop a pitch-aware network structure that adapts in a quasi-periodic manner.  Our proposed network structure utilizes three types of convolution operations: fixed, increasing, and decreasing, and we evaluate the network's performance on multiple speech synthesis tasks, including single and multi-speaker scenarios.  The results show that our proposed Network structure produces high-quality results with fewer computational costs compared to the original WaveNet model.  The source code for our proposed Network is available for public use.

  distinctions, much like how derived categories serve their categorical
  counterparts.  BiMod(A) represents the collection of all possible objects within
  the shadows framework when A is any given rigid bicategory of 1-morphisms.  A
  novel connection is established between the 2-categorical structures that can
  be built from A and those that arise from its Freyd's characteristic bicategory.

Sound localization is a challenging task for humans, particularly when trying to pinpoint distant or unfamiliar sound sources. Our brain relies on specific auditory cues, which can be misleading in certain situations, to determine the location of a sound source. In this study, we investigate how twelve participants localize sounds in a virtual acoustic environment, both in an unfamiliar setting and one they've been previously exposed to. To better understand the complexity of sound localization, we analyze our data using both continuous and discrete measures. Our findings reveal that listeners primarily use an elevation cue known as the pinna effect, which is influenced by the vertical position of the speaker, to determine the source's location. However, we also discovered that participants are more sensitive to changes in azimuth than in elevation. Moreover, our results indicate that being familiar with the setting can significantly impact sound localization performance.

Recent advancements in neural network technology have heavily relied on the use of Euclidean Neural Networks, but this approach may not be well-suited for applications where data is growing rapidly. In contrast, Neural Networks based on Lorentzian geometry have been shown to provide significant benefits in terms of performance and efficiency for certain tasks, such as graph classification. In this work, we introduce the concept of Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks, a novel method for learning from graphs that combines the benefits of neural network technology with the efficiency of Lorentzian representations. We also present a novel graph-based representation called the Hodge Sketch, which allows for fast and scalable learning using randomized algorithms. Our approach has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art results on the Amagasa dataset and comparable performance to recent state-of-the-art methods on the Amagasa and OCHRE datasets.

We propose a novel efficient exponential delay discounting model, linked to the optimization of a Tsallis entropy, which offers a more manageable alternative to traditional models. This approach yields several notable predictions, including non-linear relationships in the slopes of learning, the learning of delayed outcomes with greater difficulty, and the application of distinct learning rates to rewards and punishments.

This research presents a novel application of Weyl-Wigner quasi-probability distributions to canonical equilibrium conditions, resulting in new, non-trivial formulations. Specifically, when expressed in Weyl-Wigner representations, the balance of mass, momentum, and total energy take on unique forms. Notably, when the system is described by a non-equilibrium distribution, the balance equations manifest as non-local integral constraints on the phase space. In contrast, when expressed in terms of density, velocity, and temperature fields, these integral constraints appear as seemingly unrelated conditions. A particular model, when analyzed, yields distinct, non-trivial, and non-linear differential equations within their respective formulations.

The notion of negative absolute temperature, first introduced by Willard Gibbs in 1901, has been given a more concrete significance. In this framework, temperature is understood as a comparative measure of the rates of two distinct processes. Our analysis demonstrates that within any given reference frame, temperature corresponds to the ratio of the durations of these processes, and we propose a mathematical framework based on the Fenchel-Young inequality to better understand and work with negative absolute temperatures.

By extending the Standard Model with singlet scalars and vectors, we have developed a minimal "scoto-seesaw" model that simultaneously accounts for neutrino mass generation, electroweak symmetry breaking, and dark matter. Our analysis of the model's scoto-seesaw variant, first performed with only complex singlet scalars, is now re-examined using two types of neutral scalar fields. Our study involves investigating dark matter phenomenology, ensuring the theory remains self-consistent, and checking for holographic properties and perturbative properties. Our results show that the probability distribution of scalar fields has two distinct minima, leading to two possible vacuum states. Our analysis of dark matter phenomenology reveals that weakly interacting massive particle-like behavior emerges from tree-level exchanges of vector mediators, while radiative corrections to the Higgs potential remain within perturbative limits. Our findings also highlight the importance of vector interactions in maintaining vacuum stability. Our calculations show that the range of Higgs self-coupling parameter consistency is significantly broadened, from 0.006 to 0.016. Our study further demonstrates that dark matter can be produced via interactions with the initial Big Bang, matching observed dark matter abundance, while neutrino masses align with experimental data. Our research highlights the feasibility of detecting new physics at the Large Hadron Collider through searches for dark matter, neutrinoless double beta decay, and deviations in rare particle interactions.

In this paper, we investigate the blending of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals that results from crystal field splitting and angular effects. We examine how orbital interactions affect various physical properties in transition metal compounds. Blended orbitals are essential to consider in compounds with significant spin-orbit coupling, particularly those involving $t_{2g}$ electrons like 4d and 5d transition metals. We explore the impact of blended orbitals on various phenomena, including double exchange magnetism, band structure, and unconventional superconductivity. We also highlight recent discoveries of $e_g$-based physics in compounds with $t_{2g}$ electrons and discuss the intricate interplay of multiple influences on the $e_g$-like states.

This research introduces a novel invariant for quasi-projective 3-fold varieties under endomorphisms known as relative quantum topology. In contrast to the standard relative topology variant, this new framework produces integer values and remains unchanged under endomorphisms variously including birational transformations. It is demonstrated that this new relative quantum topology variant remains consistent under endomorphisms for certain compact quasi-projective Calabi-Yau 3-f varieties with no boundary. Interestingly, this new framework reveals distinct values for a family of non-algebraically equivalent quasi-projective varieties under the identity map, thus serving as a new type of obstructions to the algebraic equivalence of field extensions.

The concept of image generation has been extensively studied in recent years, 
with various applications being demonstrated. 
However, an interesting challenge arises when it comes to generating medical 
images that accurately reflect a specific illness. 
This is known as illness-aware image generation, and it is particularly 
important in the medical field. 
In this study, we focus on a specific aspect of this problem, which is 
controlling the intensity of a certain illness in lung X-rays through a 
method called illumination. 
This is a novel and under-explored area of research. 
We believe that our approach is also applicable to other types of medical 
images, including MRI and CT scans. 
To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted several experiments 
on the open X-ray dataset. 
The results show that our approach successfully produces images that have a 
higher alignment with the original images in terms of visual appearance, 
semantic content, and disease severity compared to the baseline approach.

This paper introduces ViDaExpert, an innovative graphical utility designed for multidimensional vector data visualization and analysis. Unlike conventional examination methods that involve sequential animation of vectors, ViDaExpert employs nonlinear examination techniques, including various space-filling curves and helical structures. These innovative approaches offer distinct advantages over traditional methods, facilitating a more efficient identification of anomalies and pattern correlations within vector data. ViDaExpert supports interactive 2D/3D visualization, customizable color-coding, automatic outlier detection, and the capability to save and replay examinations, making it a versatile tool for a wide range of examination scenarios.
